one_liner: Small C99 library for byte-oriented uint32 compression (SIMD Group Varint variant) that decodes faster than VByte, MaskedVByte and varint-G8IU.
what_it_does: Encodes arrays of 32-bit unsigned integers in 1 to 4 bytes each, with all 2-bit length codes stored in a separate control stream ahead of the data bytes, and decodes them back; optional differential coding (streamvbyte_delta_encode/decode with a starting value) for sorted input, zigzag helpers for signed input, and a 0/1/2/4-byte variant for zero-heavy data. The API is a handful of plain C functions over caller-allocated buffers (streamvbyte_encode(in, n, out) returns bytes written; streamvbyte_decode(in, out, n) returns bytes read). It is not wire-compatible with protobuf-style varint or with VByte streams, and the integer count is not stored in the stream.
how_it_is_fast: Stream VByte separates the control bytes from the data bytes, so the decoder reads one control byte (four 2-bit lengths), looks up a 16-byte shuffle mask and a length in 256-entry tables, and expands four integers with a single PSHUFB (SSE4.1) or TBL (NEON) instruction, with no per-integer branches and no dependency of the next control byte on the data. Encoding is vectorized the same way in reverse. The x64 delta decoder fuses an in-register prefix sum (two shift-and-add steps per four integers) into the decode loop. CPU features are detected at runtime, so one binary picks SSE4.1 or the scalar fallback.
when_to_use: Decode-heavy 32-bit integer arrays (posting lists, doc IDs, column chunks, tile coordinates) where you want multi-GB/s decoding and can accept byte-granular compression.
Sorted ID lists on x86-64: the delta codec has a fused SSE4.1 decode; issue #47 on the TurboPFor repo measured StreamVByte delta at 14,101.75 MB/s decode on doc IDs.
Mixed-magnitude values where bit-packing per block wastes space on outliers but you still want branch-free SIMD decode.
C or C++ projects that want a tiny, dependency-free, Apache-2.0 codec with runtime dispatch, already used by RediSearch, StarRocks, fbthrift and tilemaker per the README.
when_not_to_use: When compression ratio matters most: byte granularity costs bits versus bit-packing (the verifier's TurboPFor tables show about 10.00 vs 8.17 bits/integer against VByte on ZIPF and 11.50 vs 8.96 on gov2); FastPFor/simdcomp/TurboPFor pack tighter.
64-bit integers: the API is uint32_t only.

Delta-coded or 0124 streams on ARM64: the differential decoder and the 0124 decoder have SSE4.1 paths only, so AArch64 falls back to scalar code (open issue #17, port differential coding to NEON, since 2017).
Big-endian targets: unsupported per the README.
Untrusted streams without validation: decode trusts the count and control bytes; call streamvbyte_validate_stream first (added in December 2024).

integration.dependencies: none for the library; the perf benchmark (tests enabled) links sea_counters fetched through CPM
integration.min_toolchain: C99; GCC 9+, LLVM 10+, Visual Studio 2019+; CMake 3.10+ (a Linux-style Makefile is also provided)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE4.1 path selected at runtime, scalar fallback otherwise), AArch64 (NEON), other little-endian CPUs via the scalar path; Linux, macOS, Windows; big-endian unsupported
integration.thread_safety: Functions are stateless over caller buffers; the one shared state is the cached CPU-feature flag, which uses std::atomic in C++ and _Atomic in C11 (a plain static under MSVC C). Not otherwise documented.

gotchas: Decoding may read up to STREAMVBYTE_PADDING (16) bytes past the end of the compressed data, so allocate that slack on the input buffer; streamvbyte_compressedbytes does not include it, streamvbyte_max_compressedbytes does.
The number of integers is not stored in the stream; you must keep it yourself and pass it to decode, and the decoders cannot detect a wrong count unless you call streamvbyte_validate_stream.
Delta and plain streams are not interchangeable, and 0124 streams need the _0124 decoder and validator; using the wrong one silently returns garbage.
Version 3.0.0 (April 2026) followed a March 2026 fix to the SSE4.1 detection macro (PR #77); pin a recent release rather than an old vendored copy.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over MaskedVByte or varint-simd when you control the format and want the fastest byte-oriented decode with a simple C API (MaskedVByte keeps the standard VByte format, which is its reason to exist). Pick FastPFor, simdcomp or SIMDCompressionAndIntersection's S4-BP128 when you need better compression ratio or sorted-list intersection, and TurboPFor if its GPL license is acceptable and you want the widest codec menu.
verified_claims_summary: The best-documented comparison is on a competitor's page: TurboPFor issue #47 (icapp harness, Skylake i7-6700 3.4 GHz, October 2019, no compiler or flags) gives StreamVByte delta 14,101.75 MB/s decode on doc IDs vs FastPFor 7,616.66, SimdFastPFor 13,818.59 and MaskedVByte 6,507.48 MB/s, while on term frequencies plain StreamVByte (16,825.56 MB/s) roughly ties MaskedVByte (16,846.15 MB/s) and compresses worse (31.30% vs 25.12% of input). The repo's own perf tool reports about 41 GB/s decode and 27 GB/s encode on an Apple M4 Max for 500,000 random integers, with no baseline; the paper's 2x-over-varint-G8IU claim could not be opened here.
status_note: Actively maintained (3.0.0 released April 2026, commits through June 2026, CI on GCC 9-14, LLVM 12-18, macOS and Visual Studio), Apache-2.0, a few C files with no dependencies, so easy to vendor.
